title: Indexing throttle scenarios and evidence queueing
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures operational guidance for when the audit-log indexing pipeline encounters sustained ingestion pressure: how we throttle indexing, how we queue evidence objects for later processing, interaction with SIEM export backpressure, and the implications for retention tiers and RBAC v2-sensitive fields. It is an implementation-centric companion to the retention matrix (see Confluence link).

Quick TL;DR:
- If ingestion rate exceeds indexing capacity for >5m continuously, route older events into an evidence-queue (cold-indexing path) instead of dropping.
- Apply a multi-level throttle: per-tenant token bucket + cluster-wide soft-limit + schema-aware prioritization.
- SIEM export must not block primary custody; use async snapshots and exponential backoff for backpressure to external SIEMs.
- Backfills operate from the evidence-queue and must preserve original event timestamps and RBAC-sensitive field masks.

Background/context:
We support a high-volume audit event stream (authentication, admin actions, model access, infra events). Events are small JSON docs but can spike during incidents or migrations. Indexing pipeline components: collector -> preprocessing (parse, normalize, schema validation) -> partitioner -> indexers (hot/warm shards) -> export adapters (SIEM/long-term-archive). Evidence automation writes blobs (attachments, request payloads) to object store and references them from events.

Failure modes we see in the wild:
- Short-term spike: some indexers hit CPU/GPU (parse-heavy) and lag; queue grows but recovers within 10m.
- Sustained overload: indexer lag grows, memory usage increases and some nodes OOM; risk of eviction or dropped events if not throttled.
- Downstream SIEM outage: export adapter blocks on HTTP timeouts and consumes retry queues; if unbounded, can starve indexing worker threads.
- Backfill interference: large backfills compete with live indexing for I/O leading to cascading latency.

Operational policy (high-level):
1) Safety-first: never drop raw-event custody. Always ensure we have either indexed or archived the raw event in object store within 24h.
2) Degraded mode: when indexing lag > 5m for >5m across >20% of partitions -> switch to degraded ingestion where events are marked for cold ingestion and routed into evidence-queue with minimal preprocessing.
3) Retention enforcement: hot tier (30d), warm tier (180d), cold/archival (7y) for compliance events. Transition triggers are age-based and also policy-based (sensitivity, legal hold).

Detailed implementation notes:
A) Throttling strategy:
- Per-tenant token bucket: each tenant has a throughput budget derived from SLO and committed capacity. Token refill rate = negotiated qps-equivalent. When tokens exhausted, excess events go to evidence-queue.
- Cluster-wide soft-limit: monitor aggregate indexing QPS and queue depth. When >75% capacity sustained for 2m, increase per-tenant throttling aggressiveness (reduce token rates by 30%).
- Priority tiers: supercritical (security alerts, admin actions), default, low (debug/traces). Priority affects both tokens and cold-queue ordering.
- Backpressure signaling: emit throttle events to metrics (throttle.count, throttle.duration) and to tenant usage logs for billing/alerts.

B) Evidence-queue (cold-indexing path):
- Purpose: durable, ordered staging area that preserves raw payload + metadata for later reindexing/backfill.
- Storage: object store bucket per-region with partitioned prefixes: /evidence/{yyyy}/{mm}/{tenant}/{shard}/<uuid>.json. Small index-record in Kafka/Rabbit referencing object path.
- Minimal processing on write: timestamp normalization, tenant id, event id, schema version, sensitive-field-mask flag. No enrichment.
- TTL on pipeline-side pointer: pointer retained for 90d; underlying blobs retained per legal retention policy (can be longer).
- Reingestion workers read the queue with controlled parallelism and replay into indexers in off-peak windows.

C) SIEM export interaction:
- Exports run in independent lanes. On SIEM failure, adapters perform retry with bounded queueing (max 6h backlog) and checkpoint. After 6h, stop retrying to avoid resource starvation and persist manifest of undelivered snapshots for legal team.
- For compliance-critical tenants with synchronous SIEM needs, we provide a separate dedicated export worker pool bounded by tenant capacity to avoid cross-tenant impact.

D) RBAC v2 and schema/masking considerations:
- During degraded ingestion we still must honor RBAC masking for fields that are PII or highly sensitive. The evidence-queue record must include the applied mask metadata (masking_policy_id) so reindex can re-apply or redact consistently if policy changed.
- Reindex workers must consult policy service snapshot that corresponds to the event timestamp; failing that, they must fallback to the policy_id embedded in the evidence blob.

E) Backfill strategies and safe windows:
- Small backfills (<10M events): run in live cluster with very low concurrency and low IO priority during a maintenance window.
- Large backfills (>100M events): require staging cluster or dedicated backfill pool. Backfills should read from object store snapshots and write to indexers with traffic shaping.
- Backfill preflight: dry-run that validates schema, sample replay and ensures indexer CPU/disk/IO remain under target thresholds.

F) Observability and alerting knobs:
- Metrics to publish: indexing_lag_seconds (per-partition), evidence_queue_depth, evidence_blob_write_errors, siem_export_backlog_seconds, reindex_success_rate, throttle_events_by_tenant.
- Alerts (severity mapping):
  * P1: evidence_blob_write_errors > 1% over 5m (risk of lost custody)
  * P1: indexing_lag_seconds > 900s on >25% partitions for >10m
  * P2: siem_export_backlog_seconds > 21600 (6h) for any tenant
  * P3: reindex_failure_rate > 5% over 1h during backfill job
- Dashboards: indexer health, queue depth heatmap, per-tenant throttle timeline, SIEM export status.

G) Runbook (playback steps for SRE/security on detection of sustained indexing pressure):
1) Triage: confirm alerts in Grafana and correlate with producer spike (kinesis/kafka metrics) and recent deploys.
2) If indexing_lag > 900s and rising, enable degraded ingestion (feature-flag). Notify operations and tenants (automated email with trace id).
3) Check evidence-queue write rate and object store success. If object store 5xx errors -> escalate to storage team, pause reingestion.
4) If SIEM adapter backlog >6h, disable retries and create delivery-manifest artifact for legal with tenant list.
5) Schedule reindex window(s): off-peak, throttle to safe concurrency. For large backfills, provision backfill pool.
6) Post-recovery: run integrity check (sample count compare: raw events vs indexed events vs archived pointers) and file incident report.

H) Testing and verification recommendations:
- Chaos test: simulate indexer node failure and ensure degraded ingestion triggers and evidence-queue receives events without loss.
- SIEM outage test: cause adapter to 502 and confirm retry bounds and that indexing remains healthy.
- Policy drift test: migrate RBAC masking policy, then reindex a small sample from evidence-queue to verify policy snapshot usage.

I) Open questions / decisions to make:
- Exact per-tenant token allocation formula (SLO vs usage-based billing trade-offs).
- Default retention for evidence pointers vs blobs under mixed-legal-hold conditions.
- Whether to store plaintext minimal indices for fast search on cold blobs (privacy risk).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally operational; implementation details (queues, thresholds) are proposed and should be validated by infra + storage leads.
- For auditors: we must be able to demonstrate non-drop custody within 24h and provide manifest for any undelivered SIEM snapshots.

Appendix: quick checklist for an incident:
- Verify raw-event presence in object store (sample 10 events) -> ok/failed
- Check evidence-queue pointer integrity -> no missing sequence numbers
- Confirm RBAC mask metadata exists in every evidence blob -> if missing, escalate (possible compliance gap)
- If backfills are active, confirm they are running in dedicated pool with IO throttling

End of doc.

Author notes: will follow up with a companion diagram (topology + dataflows) and a small RFC for token allocation formula.
